The quiet reshaping of the American city

From empty offices to newly walkable blocks, a different urban future is taking shape.

BY MAYA ORTIZ
OCTOBER 14, 2024 · 8 MIN READ

For decades, the American city was drawn around a commute. Every morning, millions moved inward; every evening, they moved out. The map made sense because the schedule did.

Now the schedule is changing. A generation of hybrid workers has loosened the old rhythm, leaving behind a question that is both practical and profound: what should the city be for?

A city is not a machine for moving people. It is a way of keeping them close.

ESSAY / ATTENTION

The Quiet Work of Paying Attention

In an age of acceleration, noticing has become a radical form of care.

By Mara Ellison · October 12, 2024 · 18 min read

“The world does not become richer when we move faster through it.”

— Simone Weil

There is a particular kind of tiredness that arrives when every moment has been accounted for. It is not the tiredness of work, exactly, but of being asked to witness everything at once.

Attention asks for less. It asks us to stay with the cup cooling beside the book, the late light gathering on the floor, the sentence we almost skipped.

A practice of staying

To pay attention is not to collect more impressions. It is to let one impression become precise.

The ordinary is not waiting to be made extraordinary. It is waiting to be met without haste.

THE LEDGER
MONDAY, OCTOBER 14, 2024
CITIES

The quiet reshaping of the American city

From empty offices to newly walkable blocks, a different urban future is taking shape.

BY MAYA ORTIZ
OCTOBER 14, 2024 · 8 MIN READ

For decades, the American city was drawn around a commute. Every morning, millions moved inward; every evening, they moved out. The map made sense because the schedule did.

Now the schedule is changing. A generation of hybrid workers has loosened the old rhythm, leaving behind a question that is both practical and profound: what should the city be for?

In blocks once defined by glass towers and lunchtime crowds, small experiments are taking root. Libraries are extending their hours. Empty storefronts are becoming kitchens, studios, and places to meet.

A city is not a machine for moving people. It is a way of keeping them close.
— LENA MORI, URBANIST

ESSAY / ATTENTION

The Quiet Work of Paying Attention

In an age of acceleration, noticing has become a radical form of care.

By Mara Ellison · October 12, 2024 · 18 min read

“The world does not become richer when we move faster through it.”

— Simone Weil

There is a particular kind of tiredness that arrives when every moment has been accounted for. It is not the tiredness of work, exactly, but of being asked to witness everything at once.

Attention asks for less. It asks us to stay with the cup cooling beside the book, the late light gathering on the floor, the sentence we almost skipped.

A practice of staying

To pay attention is not to collect more impressions. It is to let one impression become precise.

The ordinary is not waiting to be made extraordinary. It is waiting to be met without haste.
